overview.title: Classification, segmentation, and detection
overview.main_topic: Definitions and real-world examples of the three essential computer vision tasks, illustrated by figure 11.1 on a single photo of two cyclists.
overview.central_idea: The three tasks differ in what they output. Classification assigns one or more labels to the whole image (single-label or multilabel). Segmentation partitions the image into areas, each usually a category, at pixel-level precision. Object detection draws labeled bounding boxes around objects of interest.
overview.importance: Knowing which task fits a problem decides the model architecture, the label format, the loss, and the cost of annotation. The rest of chapter 11 and chapter 12 build on these definitions.
learning_objectives: Define image classification and distinguish single-label from multilabel classification.
Define image segmentation and explain what pixel-level precision means.
Define object detection and bounding boxes.
Read the four panels of figure 11.1 and say what each output contains.
Match real applications (Google Photos search, video-call backgrounds, self-driving cars) to tasks.
prerequisites: Classification vocabulary: classes, labels, binary and multiclass classification (p.129)

summary:
The page lists the **three essential computer vision tasks** announced on p.332.

1. **Image classification**: assign one or more labels to an image. It is either *single-label* (categories mutually exclusive) or *multilabel* (tag every category the image belongs to). Example: a keyword search in the Google Photos app queries a very large multilabel classifier with **over 20,000 classes, trained on millions of images**.
2. **Image segmentation**: "segment" or "partition" the image into areas, each usually representing a category. Example: Zoom or Google Meet custom backgrounds use a segmentation model to separate you from what is behind you, **with pixel-level precision**.
3. **Object detection**: draw rectangles, called **bounding boxes**, around objects of interest and associate each with a class. Example: a self-driving car monitoring cars, pedestrians, and signs in its cameras' view.

**Figure 11.1** applies all of these to one photo of two people cycling in a park:

- *Single-label multi-class classification*: radio buttons Biking (chosen), Running, Swimming. Exactly one answer.
- *Multi-label classification*: checkboxes, with Bike, Person, and Tree ticked and Boat, Car, House not ticked. Any number of answers.
- *Image segmentation*: the two riders are filled in one color (labeled "person") and the bicycles in another ("bike"). Every pixel of those objects is assigned a class.
- *Object detection*: labeled rectangles for each person, each bike, and two street lamps.

Read together, the panels show increasing spatial detail. Classification says *what* is in the image, detection adds roughly *where* each object is, and segmentation gives the *exact shape* of each region. The next page (p.334) mentions more niche tasks (similarity scoring, keypoints, pose, depth...) and says almost every vision application reduces to one of these three.

paragraphs.excerpt: Image classification, where the goal is to assign one or more labels
paragraphs.what_it_says: Image classification assigns one or more labels to an image. It can be single-label (mutually exclusive categories) or multilabel (tag all categories the image belongs to, as in figure 11.1). Google Photos keyword search uses a very large multilabel classifier with over 20,000 classes trained on millions of images.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The whole image gets labels, with no spatial information. Whether labels are exclusive changes the problem. Single-label asks 'which one?', so the outputs compete. Multilabel asks a separate yes/no question for each class ('bike? person? tree?').
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This choice decides the output layer and the loss. The Google Photos example shows that multilabel classification at scale is a production technology behind everyday search.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book (consistent with chapter 4): single-label uses a softmax output with categorical crossentropy, so probabilities sum to 1. Multilabel uses one sigmoid per class with binary crossentropy, so each class is an independent probability. With 20,000 classes, each photo can match many search keywords at once.

terminology.meaning: Each image belongs to exactly one of several mutually exclusive categories.
Each image can carry any number of labels at once.

connections: p.129: classification glossary (classes, labels, binary vs multiclass vs multilabel).
p.332: classification as 'an image goes in, a label comes out'.

paragraphs.excerpt: Image segmentation, where the goal is to “segment” or “partition” an image
paragraphs.what_it_says: Image segmentation partitions an image into areas, each usually representing a category (figure 11.1). Zoom or Google Meet custom backgrounds use segmentation to separate your face from what is behind it, with pixel-level precision.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of one answer per image, the model gives one answer per pixel. The output is a mask with the same height and width as the image. The video-call example is binary (person vs background), but the same idea extends to many categories.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Segmentation is the subject of this chapter. It powers editing, autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging (p.334), wherever exact shapes and boundaries matter.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: semantic segmentation can be framed as classifying every pixel, giving an output of shape (H, W, num_classes) trained with a per-pixel crossentropy. Section 11.2 builds such a model from strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers (p.352).

terminology.meaning: An image-sized map that assigns a class (or instance) to every pixel.
Region boundaries follow object outlines exactly, down to individual pixels.

connections: p.334: segmentation as assigning a class to each pixel, and its three flavors (semantic, instance, panoptic).
p.352: chapter summary on building a segmentation model with Conv2D and Conv2DTranspose stacks.

paragraphs.excerpt: Object detection, where the goal is to draw rectangles (called bounding boxes)
paragraphs.what_it_says: Object detection draws rectangles (bounding boxes) around objects of interest and associates each with a class. A self-driving car could use it to monitor cars, pedestrians, and signs in view of its cameras.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output is a variable-length list of (box, class) pairs, often with a confidence score. Boxes give location and rough extent but not exact shape.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Detection handles counting, tracking, and localization at lower cost than segmentation. Chapter 12 explains that segmentation is a strict superset of detection but is slower to run and much more expensive to label (p.354).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a box is usually encoded as four numbers (for example, x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max, or center x, center y, width, height). Since the number of objects varies per image, detectors predict many candidate boxes and filter them.

terminology.meaning: An axis-aligned rectangle enclosing an object, given by four coordinates.
An instance of one of the classes the detector was trained to find.

connections: p.353: chapter 12 opener, with counting, tracking, and cropping as detection applications.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 11.1 The three main computer vision tasks: classification, segmentation, and detection
paragraphs.what_it_says: Four panels on the same cycling photo: single-label multi-class classification (Biking chosen over Running and Swimming), multi-label classification (Bike, Person, Tree ticked; Boat, Car, House not ticked), image segmentation (riders colored as 'person', bicycles as 'bike'), and object detection (boxes labeled person, bike, and street lamp).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Classification is shown twice because of the single-label/multilabel distinction. The segmentation panel is semantic: both people share one color and one label. The detection panel separates individual instances (two 'person' boxes) but gives only rectangles, which overlap and include background pixels.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing one input under four output formats is the clearest way to understand how the tasks differ in granularity and in what they leave out.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note that the street lamps appear only in the detection panel and the tree only in the multilabel list. Each task's output depends on the class set it was trained with, not just on what is in the photo (interpretation).

terminology.meaning: The figure's visual metaphor: radio buttons mean one exclusive choice (single-label), and checkboxes mean any subset (multilabel).

connections: p.334: figure 11.2 contrasts semantic and instance segmentation, explaining why both riders share a color here.

concepts.name: Image classification
concepts.definition: Assigning one or more labels to an entire image, either single-label (mutually exclusive) or multilabel (all categories that apply).
concepts.intuition: Answering 'what is in this picture?' without saying where.
concepts.technical: Output is a vector over classes: softmax for single-label, independent sigmoids for multilabel (beyond the book on this page).
concepts.significance: The task covered in chapter 8 and the base the other tasks build on.
concepts.example: Google Photos search: a multilabel model with over 20,000 classes.
concepts.misconception: That classification always picks exactly one class. Multilabel classification tags all that apply.

concepts.name: Multilabel classification
concepts.definition: Tagging an image with every category it belongs to; labels are not mutually exclusive.
concepts.intuition: A checklist, not a multiple-choice question.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: one sigmoid output per class with binary crossentropy, and a decision threshold (for example, 0.5) per class.
concepts.significance: Matches real photos, which usually contain many things at once.
concepts.example: Figure 11.1: Bike, Person, and Tree are all ticked for the same photo.
concepts.misconception: That you can get multilabel predictions by taking the top-k of a softmax. Softmax forces classes to compete, which is wrong when several are present at full confidence.

concepts.name: Image segmentation
concepts.definition: Partitioning an image into areas, each usually representing a category, at pixel-level precision.
concepts.intuition: Coloring in every object in a coloring book with the color of its class.
concepts.technical: Output is a mask of the image's height and width with a class per pixel (and, for instance segmentation, an instance id; p.334).
concepts.significance: Main topic of chapter 11. It gives exact shapes, unlike boxes.
concepts.example: Video-call background replacement separating the person from the background.
concepts.misconception: That segmentation is just detection with smaller boxes. It labels individual pixels and so captures arbitrary shapes.

concepts.name: Object detection
concepts.definition: Drawing bounding boxes around objects of interest and assigning each box a class.
concepts.intuition: Putting a labeled frame around everything important.
concepts.technical: Output is a variable-size set of (box coordinates, class, score) entries. Covered in chapter 12.
concepts.significance: Cheaper than segmentation to label and run, and enough when pixel precision is not needed (p.354).
concepts.example: A self-driving car tracking cars, pedestrians, and signs.
concepts.misconception: That detection tells you an object's exact shape. A box also contains background pixels.

concepts.name: Bounding box
concepts.definition: A rectangle drawn around an object of interest.
concepts.intuition: The smallest picture frame that fits around the object.
concepts.technical: Typically encoded by four numbers. From an instance mask you can compute the tightest box, but not the other way around (p.354).
concepts.significance: The unit of output and annotation in object detection.
concepts.misconception: That boxes can't overlap. In figure 11.1 the person and bike boxes overlap heavily.

deeper.title: Same photo, four output formats
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, approximate output structures for figure 11.1's photo, assuming an H × W image:

| task | output | example from fig. 11.1 |
|---|---|---|
| single-label | 1 probability vector, sums to 1 | Biking 0.97, Running 0.02, Swimming 0.01 |
| multilabel | 1 independent probability per class | Bike 0.98, Person 0.99, Tree 0.95, Car 0.03 ... |
| segmentation | H × W class map | each pixel ∈ {background, person, bike} |
| detection | list of (box, class, score) | 2 × person, 2 × bike, 2 × street lamp |

The probabilities are invented to show the formats. The labels are those printed in the figure.

deeper.title: Why video calls need segmentation, not detection
deeper.body: To replace the background behind you, the software must decide for each pixel whether it is you or the room. A bounding box around your head and shoulders would include patches of wall in the corners, which would stay visible and look wrong. That is why the book says such tools work with pixel-level precision. A detector would be enough for a different job, such as framing the camera on you (auto-zoom). (Interpretation built on the book's example.)

deeper.title: Increasing spatial detail
deeper.body: Think of describing a crowd photo to someone over the phone. Classification: "there are people and bikes." Detection: "one person is in the upper middle, another to the right, and there are bikes under them." Segmentation: you trace every outline on a transparent sheet. Each step costs more effort (and, for models, more computation and labeling) but gives more information.

misconceptions.claim: Image classification always returns a single label.
misconceptions.correction: It may be single-label or multilabel. Google Photos search uses a multilabel model with over 20,000 classes.

misconceptions.claim: Object detection gives the exact outline of each object.
misconceptions.correction: It gives rectangles (bounding boxes). Exact outlines require segmentation.

misconceptions.claim: The segmentation panel of figure 11.1 distinguishes the two riders.
misconceptions.correction: Both riders share the 'person' color, which is semantic segmentation. Distinguishing them is instance segmentation, defined on p.334.

misconceptions.claim: Segmentation and detection are unrelated tasks.
misconceptions.correction: Segmentation is a strict superset of detection: a box can be computed from an instance mask, but segmentation costs more to run and to label (p.354).

takeaways: Image classification assigns one or more labels to a whole image, either single-label (exclusive) or multilabel (all that apply).
Google Photos search is a multilabel classifier with over 20,000 classes trained on millions of images.
Image segmentation partitions an image into areas, usually one category each, with pixel-level precision (for example, video-call backgrounds).
Object detection draws labeled bounding boxes around objects of interest (for example, self-driving cars).
Figure 11.1 shows the same photo under all four output formats, with spatial detail increasing from labels to boxes to masks.

questions.question: In figure 11.1, which panel uses checkboxes with Bike, Person, and Tree ticked?
questions.explanation: Checkboxes mean several labels can apply at once. The single-label panel uses radio buttons (Biking). The segmentation panel uses colored masks, and the detection panel uses rectangles.

questions.question: What is the difference between single-label and multilabel classification, according to the page?
questions.answer: In single-label classification the categories are mutually exclusive, so the image gets exactly one. In multilabel classification you tag all categories the image belongs to.

questions.question: Which application does the book use to illustrate image segmentation?
options: Custom backgrounds in Zoom or Google Meet video calls
Monitoring cars, pedestrians, and signs from a self-driving car
Estimating how visually similar two images are
questions.answer: Custom backgrounds in Zoom or Google Meet video calls
questions.explanation: The book's segmentation example separates you from your background with pixel-level precision. Google Photos illustrates multilabel classification, self-driving cars illustrate detection, and similarity scoring is a niche task listed on p.334.

questions.question: For each of the following, which task fits best, and why? (a) counting pedestrians crossing a street, (b) measuring the area of a tumor in a medical scan, (c) tagging vacation photos with keywords.
questions.answer: (a) Object detection: counting needs individual instances, not exact shapes, and detection is cheaper. (b) Segmentation: area needs the exact outline at pixel level. (c) Multilabel classification: you need all applicable tags for the whole image, with no location.
questions.explanation: Applies the definitions on this page. The counting example matches p.353-354, where detection is preferred when pixel-level information is not needed.

questions.question: In figure 11.1 both riders share the same color in the segmentation panel, but the detection panel draws two separate 'person' boxes. What does this tell you about the two outputs?
questions.answer: The segmentation shown is semantic: it labels pixels by category only, so the two people merge into one 'person' class. Detection outputs one box per instance, so it separates individuals but only gives rough rectangles rather than shapes.
questions.explanation: This prepares the semantic vs instance distinction on p.334.

questions.question: How many classes does the book say the Google Photos multilabel model has, and what is it trained on?
questions.answer: Over 20,000 classes, trained on millions of images.

questions.question: Can you sketch, for one photo of your choice, what a single-label, multilabel, segmentation, and detection output would look like?
questions.answer: Self-check: you should produce one exclusive label, a set of ticked labels, a per-pixel colored mask, and a set of labeled rectangles, as in figure 11.1.
questions.explanation: Reproducing figure 11.1 on a new image checks that you understand all four formats.
